slides.headline: Ostriches never bury their heads in sand.
slides.sub: So where did the idea come from? Two very ordinary habits

slides.headline: Down, flat and very still
slides.body: If danger comes and it cannot run, an ostrich may drop to the ground and lie still, neck stretched flat. From far off, the head seems to vanish.
slides.source: Britannica; San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance

slides.headline: Head in the nest, not the sand
slides.body: The nest is a shallow scrape in the ground. Tending it, ostriches dip their heads low to turn the eggs, which may explain the myth.

slides.label: top sprint speed, in short bursts
slides.body: Running, not hiding, is its main escape. Scientists have seen ostriches keep up 48–59 km/h continuously.
slides.source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance; Smithsonian

slides.label: across: the size of each eye, the largest of any bird
slides.body: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance goes further: the largest eye of any land animal.

slides.headline: The biggest bird alive
slides.body: Males stand up to 2.7 m tall and weigh up to 130 kg. The IUCN rates it Least Concern (2025), though wild numbers have declined.

caption:
Ostriches do not bury their heads in sand: the common ostrich (Struthio camelus) lies flat or dips into its nest instead.

The nest is a communal scrape in the ground shared by several hens. The male usually sits on the eggs at night and the females take turns by day, and every so often a bird lowers its head to turn them. Chicks use the lie-flat trick too, and if cornered an adult can deliver a dangerous kick with its two-toed feet.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.
